title: Decode Ways
statement: Letters are encoded as numbers: 'A' is 1, 'B' is 2, ... 'Z' is 26. Given a string of digits, count how many different letter strings could have produced it. A code is read one or two digits at a time; a two-digit code must be between 10 and 26, and a code never has a leading zero, so '0' alone and '06' are not valid codes.
realWorld: Counting the consistent parses of an ambiguous variable-width encoding — a billing or telemetry record where a field may occupy one or two bytes and the reader must decide how many interpretations a stream admits before rejecting it as ambiguous. The same counting shape appears in tokenising text against an ambiguous grammar.

examples.explanation: 2|2|6 = 'BBF', 22|6 = 'VF', 2|26 = 'BZ'. Note 226 itself is not a code — codes are one or two digits.
Only 2|10|1 works. The 0 cannot stand alone, so it must join the 1 before it as 10; and '01' is not a valid two-digit code, so the final 1 must stand alone.

constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer
A leading zero makes a code invalid: '0', '01' and '06' are not codes

bruteForce.idea: Recursively consume the string from the left: at each position take one digit as a code if it is not '0', and take two digits if they form a number between 10 and 26. Add up the counts from both branches.
code: private static int count(String s, int i) {
if (i == s.length()) return 1;   // consumed the whole string: one valid decoding
bruteForce.whySlow: Every position forks into a one-digit and a two-digit branch, so on a string like '1111111111...' the call tree is Fibonacci-shaped and count(i) is evaluated once for every way the prefix before i can be cut. For a 40-digit string of 1s that is about 10^8 calls, and count(38) alone is reached hundreds of millions of times — always returning the same number, because the number of decodings of a suffix cannot depend on how the prefix was split.

patternIdentification: The answer for the whole string is a sum over the ways the last code could have been formed — one digit, or two — and each of those refers back to the answer for a shorter prefix. That is the tell for a one-dimensional DP indexed by prefix length. Say the state out loud first: dp[i] = the number of ways to decode the first i characters. The recurrence follows by asking what the final code was: dp[i] = dp[i-1] if the last digit can stand alone, plus dp[i-2] if the last two digits form a code in 10..26. The base cases are dp[0] = 1 (the empty prefix has exactly one decoding: take no codes at all) and dp[1] = 1 unless the first character is '0'. Structurally this is climbing stairs — 'reach i from i-1 or i-2' — with a validity test on each move; recognising a familiar recurrence under a new set of legality rules is most of what DP fluency is.

optimized.idea: Fill dp left to right over prefix lengths. The two terms are guarded independently: the one-digit term only counts when the last digit is not '0', and the two-digit term only when the pair is between 10 and 26 — which rejects both 'over 26' and 'leading zero' with a single range test. Only dp[i-1] and dp[i-2] are ever read, so two ints suffice.
code: int twoBack = 1;   // dp[0]: the empty prefix has exactly one decoding
int oneBack = 1;   // dp[1]: the first digit is not '0', so it stands alone
if (pair >= 10 && pair <= 26) ways += twoBack;   // >= 10 is what rejects '06'

commonMistakes: Letting '0' stand as its own code by adding dp[i-1] unconditionally. '06' then returns 1 instead of 0 and '10' returns 2 instead of 1 — the count is inflated on exactly the inputs a test suite is least likely to include.

Testing only pair <= 26 and forgetting pair >= 10, so '01' is accepted as the letter A. The input '101' returns 2 where the answer is 1, because the bogus split 1|01 is counted alongside the real 10|1.

Setting dp[0] = 0 on the grounds that an empty string has nothing to decode. Every two-digit code that consumes the first two characters then contributes zero, and '12' returns 1 instead of 2 while longer inputs come out uniformly too small.
